Everyone believes in their own inflated ability to manage the enormous financial risks that are baked into the financial markets today.

But the people who survive monetary resets — and there have been dozens of monetary resets, in every century of every civilization — are never the cleverest traders. They are not the ones with the best read on the next Fed meeting. They are not the stock pickers or the options hedgers or the macro gurus. 

Those are the people who get wiped out. 

To survive the Fourth Turning and the coming global monetary reset, you must learn how to structure your capital in ways that are profoundly resilient. The objective when you are building a resilient strategy is not to guess the future. It is to be prepared for whatever happens next, because the one thing you can know for sure is that a bankrupt government will do everything it can to destroy you in an effort to save itself.

There is such a financial architecture. It has a name and a genealogy. It was invented almost 50 years ago by a man I knew personally, Harry Browne. I have spent the last 25 years refining this strategy at the edges, as new evidence has come in and as the monetary landscape has evolved.

Harry Browne died in 2006. That was 2 years before Lehman Brothers. It was 15 years before the COVID panic. And 20 years before the Fourth Turning had become inevitable. He was not here to see the forty-year bull market in bonds break. He was not here to see central banks resume buying gold at record pace after a generation of selling. He was not here to see Bitcoin emerge as digital gold. He was not here to see the 60/40 portfolio fail. 

But Harry’s framework — the four asset classes, the equal weights, the discipline of holding through every kind of season — is exactly the right framework for the world he did not live to see, and a testament to his genius.

I have spent 28 years applying Harry’s principle, modified by the Davis insight about insurance, sharpened by the Lindy Effect, anchored by gold and Bitcoin, and disciplined by active cash management. The result is the most resilient long-term portfolio I know how to build. 

With the help of Matt Tuttle, there's now an ETF that's managed using my version of Harry's Permanent Portfolio strategy.

On November 3, 2009, Warren Buffett announced that Berkshire Hathaway would acquire Burlington Northern Santa Fe for $26.5 billion.
This was about six months after the market made its lows following the Global Financial Crisis, making BNSF the signature Berkshire investment of the crisis.
Berkshire had been quietly accumulating BNSF stock in the open market since August 2006, three years earlier. It already owned 22.5% of the railroad. The position could have been built out quarter by quarter, share by share, at market prices, in the same way Buffett built Berkshire’s position in Coca-Cola 20 years earlier. He chose not to. On November 3, he telephoned Matt Rose, BNSF’s CEO, and offered to buy the remaining 77.5% in a single transaction at $100 per share. And Berkshire, at that moment, locked itself into a transaction whose full arithmetic the financial press has never properly understood.
Here is the deal, in numbers.
Consideration for the 77.5% Berkshire did not already own: $26.5 billion. Of that, $15.9 billion was paid in cash. Of that cash, roughly half was drawn from Berkshire’s balance sheet, and the other half — about $8 billion — was raised through new corporate debt issued at the Berkshire parent level. The remaining $10.6 billion of the purchase price was paid in Berkshire stock.
Buffett issued 80,931 Class A shares and 20,976,621 Class B shares to buy his railroad. At the $80,000-per-share level at which Berkshire traded that day, those shares were worth $10.6 billion. At today’s price, the same shares are worth approximately $73 billion.
Later, Buffett would write about the deal: 
“In our BNSF acquisition, the selling shareholders quite properly evaluated our offer at $100 per share. The cost to us, however, was somewhat higher since 40% of the $100 was delivered in our shares, which Charlie and I believed to be worth more than their market value.”
That's the understatement of his career. 
That $73 billion — the present-day value of what Berkshire gave up in it own shares — is larger than the entire current market capitalization of Union Pacific. It is larger than the combined current market cap of CSX and Norfolk Southern.
Buffett used the best currency in capitalism to buy the worst-performing asset in its industry, and then he committed Berkshire to spending $22 billion of additional capital over the next fourteen years just to keep the asset running in place.

And this huge mistake is about to get a lot worse. 

In his 2023 letter, Buffett wrote that BNSF’s dividends to Berkshire “will regularly fall considerably short of BNSF’s reported earnings unless we regularly increase the railroad’s debt. And that we do not intend to do.”
Translated: Berkshire had been using BNSF’s balance sheet to finance a portion of its capital shortfalls each year. Now, when BNSF needs more capital than it produces, it will not be able to add any further debt. For fourteen years, a meaningful share of BNSF’s annual capital budget has come from the credit markets. Buffett has now drawn the line. The debt will not grow further.
That decision has a consequence that does not appear in any Berkshire annual letter. If BNSF cannot add incremental debt, and if BNSF’s capital expenditures continue to exceed depreciation by a billion dollars or more every year, then BNSF’s dividends to Berkshire have to fall. Either capex gets cut — with predictable consequences for a physical network whose core asset is already compounding at a slower rate than its depreciation — or the dividends shrink. There is no third option.
The dividends have already begun to shrink. In 2020, BNSF paid Berkshire $4.8 billion. In 2022, $5.0 billion. In 2023, it fell to $3.1 billion. In 2024, it recovered to $4.0 billion — still below 2020. The cumulative 2010-through-2020 distributions Buffett so proudly cited in the 2020 letter — “$41.8 billion in total” — averaged roughly $3.8 billion a year across that decade. The 2023 and 2024 figures are running at or below that long-run average, despite inflation, despite revenue growth, despite fourteen years of capital-expenditure investment that was supposed to compound into higher earnings power.
The capital went in. Most of it did not come back out. And more and more of it never will

Between 1965 and 1999 — Buffett’s first 35 years running Berkshire — the company beat the S&P 500 in roughly 80% of the individual years measured. The average annual outperformance was an incredible 11 percentage points.
Between 2000 and 2025, the 26 years since the General Re acquisition and the pivot to owning private companies, Berkshire beat the S&P 500 in 16 of 26 years. The average annual outperformance dropped to 4.8 percentage points — less than half the prior margin.
Since 2016 and Berkshire’s full evolution into the industrial conglomerate it is today, the company has beaten the S&P 500 in only six of ten years. The average annual outperformance over the last decade is 2.4 percentage points. 
Why? What has changed about Berkshire? It isn't merely its size. What changed was its strategy. It became a conglomerate.
The General Re deal was the first crack in Buffett’s capital allocation discipline -- because he paid in stock! That broke the rule Buffett had preached for two decades: never issue Berkshire shares for less than their intrinsic value. 
By 1999 Buffett was willing to make exceptions to his own rule when the acquisition was large enough to matter and when there was a huge amount of float to be gained. That was a psychological shift, a shift in temperament. And that shift would define the next 25 years at Berkshire.
The second crack arrived almost immediately. In 1999, Berkshire made no significant new stock purchases. The tech bubble was at its peak. The S&P 500 returned 21% that year, on top of 28.6% the year before. Berkshire returned negative 19.9% — the worst relative year in its corporate history. Buffett was widely mocked as a dinosaur who had missed the internet revolution. His response was characteristic. He held the Inevitables. He did not chase tech. He did not sell what he owned.
But he also did not buy. And this is the part the financial press missed entirely.
The General Re acquisition put an enormous amount of additional float ($14 billion) into Buffett’s hands. Thus, by 1999, Buffett had roughly $27 billion in float, growing at $3 billion a year. Roughly half of it was sitting in cash. The Inevitables were fully valued at that point — Coca-Cola was trading at 40 times earnings, Gillette at 35 times, American Express at 25 times. The stocks Buffett had made his career buying cheap were no longer cheap.
A disciplined allocator with roughly $20 billion of cash and no attractive public-equity opportunities had three choices. He could let the cash accumulate on Berkshire’s balance sheet, earning the Treasury-bill rate, until something became cheap again. He could return the excess capital to shareholders through a special dividend or a share buyback. Or he could invest the capital somewhere else.
Buffett chose a fourth option that did not exist on that list. He began buying whole private companies.
In 1999 he bought Jordan’s Furniture and NetJets, the latter for $725 million. In 2000 he acquired Ben Bridge Jeweler, Justin Industries, Benjamin Moore, and Shaw Industries. In 2001 Berkshire acquired MiTek, H&R Block, and XTRA. In 2002 he bought Fruit of the Loom out of bankruptcy and the Pampered Chef from its founder. By the end of 2003 the roster of wholly-owned Berkshire subsidiaries had tripled from where it stood in 1998, and the company’s capital was increasingly tied up in operating businesses whose returns on capital and dividend yields bore no resemblance to the Inevitables.
This was when the machine began to break. Not the 2008 crisis. Not Precision Castparts in 2016. Not BNSF in 2010. The problems started in 1999 and 2000, in the twelve months after General Re, when Warren Buffett, at 69 years old, decided that he would rather buy whole mediocre businesses than wait patiently for great public businesses to become cheap again. 
The same man. The same insurance float. The same underwriting culture. The same stock-picking strategy. The same patience. The same principles. But not the same temperament. Buffett was no longer content to sit back and let other CEOs do the work.
Before 1999, Berkshire’s incremental capital went to Coca-Cola and American Express and Moody’s and Washington Post. After 1999, Berkshire’s incremental capital went to Dairy Queen and NetJets and Benjamin Moore and Clayton Homes — and eventually to BNSF and Berkshire Hathaway Energy and Precision Castparts.
It was like watching a man who only shopped at Tiffany’s bring home a fake diamond from Zales. Not even Buffett could transform a bunch of also-rans into Inevitables. And those mistakes would end up costing Berkshire Hathaway shareholders nearly as much in opportunity costs over the last 25 years as Buffett had earned them in the first 35.

Here's what will trigger the next crisis... 

The federal government is not just the largest institution in America. It is larger than any private institution by at least a factor of 10.

All state and local governments combined spend around $3.7 trillion annually. Seems like a lot of money. But it's only half of federal outlays. 

The largest U.S. corporations have annual revenue in the low hundreds of billions. Even the very largest private or quasi‑public systems (hospital groups, universities, Fortune 10 firms) are one order of magnitude (10x) smaller than the federal budget taken alone.

A leviathan spiraling toward insolvency with a printing press, isn’t going to suddenly become chaste. It is going to defraud its creditors. And it is going to force the world to continue to take its worthless currency.

It has happened before.

In October 1973 Egypt and Syria attacked Israel on the Jewish holiday Yom Kippur. The United States resupplied Israel, and the Arab oil producers answered with an embargo. Oil ran from $3 a barrel to nearly $12 in a matter of weeks, a 300% increase.

What Americans were never told was that America’s involvement in this war was never about Israel. It was always a war over the dollar. Israel was only the battleground.

Before 1971, OPEC oil was paid for in U.S. dollars. That’s because the dollar was the center of the Bretton Woods currency agreement: it was as good as gold. But after Nixon defaulted on that promise in August 1971, the Saudis demanded the U.S. honor the gold price for its oil. And they threatened to trade oil in other currencies if we didn’t. The war proved to the Saudis and the other OPEC nations they had no choice: accept the dollar or face destruction. The U.S. and Saudi Arabia secretly struck an agreement where Saudi oil would continue to be sold for dollars and Saudi surpluses would be recycled into dollar assets, especially U.S. Treasuries. In return, we guaranteed the Saudis’ sovereignty – most importantly, we promised to protect them from Iran.

This agreement held until the massive COVID inflation. After we printed $5 trillion in a year, senior Saudi officials began publicly saying at the World Economic Forum in Davos and elsewhere that they were open to settling oil trade in currencies other than the dollar, breaking the greenback monopoly. And in 2024 Saudi Arabia quietly let its old, informal understanding about pricing oil exclusively in dollars lapse, signaling that, while most deals still clear in dollars, the Saudi kingdom reserves the right to accept other currencies, especially China’s yuan, for at least some exports.

Today, about 25% of the world’s oil is priced in Chinese yuan – not dollars. The leading non‑dollar exporter? Iran.

Don’t watch the news. Watch the money.

What this war is really about is ensuring that the Saudis (and the rest of the Arab Gulf) cannot leave the dollar system. But will that work this time? And at what cost? The market doesn’t know.

Brent crude oil is sharply higher this year. Analysts at major banks are modeling $120 to $150 a barrel global oil prices if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed for much longer. Energy inflation in the latest American data runs at 17.9%, and it is dragging the headline inflation rate back up. War, then oil, then inflation. That was the sequence in 1973.

It will happen again. And, once again, the U.S. monetary authorities will monetize the spiraling costs, leading to vastly higher rates of inflation.

Here’s what happened last time.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average peaked at just over 1,000 in January 1973. It bottomed at 577 in December 1974, a fall of 45%. The S&P 500 lost about 15% in 1973 and then another 26% in 1974. Real GDP swung from +7.2% in 1972 to –2.1% in 1974. Inflation ran from 3.4% to 12.3%. The unemployment rate doubled.

The Nifty Fifty, the unkillable one‑decision stocks, were slaughtered. Their multiples collapsed from 42x earnings to under 10x earnings. Polaroid fell 91%. Avon fell 86%. Xerox fell 71%. The market did not reclaim its 1973 high, in nominal terms, until 1981. In real terms (adjusted for inflation) the market didn’t recover for 25 years.

Today the bubble is more concentrated. The deficits and the debt are vastly larger. The government is vastly more powerful and far more desperate to maintain its fiscal hegemony over the world’s economy. Loudoun County, Virginia – outside of Washington, D.C. – has been the richest county in the United States since just after the Global Financial Crisis. It will destroy the entire country to remain so.

The crisis hasn’t happened yet. The labor market is booming. The economy is growing fast. You’ll see headline after headline going into the elections this fall that America’s economy is the strongest it has ever been.
